items.stem: An online store uses Amazon DynamoDB for its orders table. The partition key of the table is CustomerId, and the sort key is OrderDate. A new screen in the application must list the orders of one customer sorted by OrderTotal. The table currently holds two years of orders, and eventually consistent reads are acceptable. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: currently holds two years of orders

options.text: Add a global secondary index with CustomerId as the partition key and OrderTotal as the sort key, and query the index for the screen.
options.why: You can [add a new global secondary index](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-index-online-operations-gsi-vs-lsi) to a table that holds data, and [the table continues to be available](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-gsi-add-to-existing-table) during the build.

options.text: Define a local secondary index on the table with OrderTotal as the sort key, and query the index for the screen.
options.why: The table already holds orders, and you [cannot add a local secondary index](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-index-online-operations-gsi-vs-lsi) to an existing table.

options.text: Scan the table with a filter expression on CustomerId for each request, and sort the returned orders by OrderTotal in the application.
options.why: It works, but a Scan [consumes the same amount of read capacity](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-scan-filter-same-read-capacity) with or without a filter, so each screen reads every order.

options.text: Copy each order into a second table keyed by CustomerId and OrderTotal through a Lambda function that reads the stream of the table.
options.why: It works, but the team writes and runs a function and a second table, while [DynamoDB maintains indexes automatically](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-indexes-maintained-automatically).
options.misconception: builds a copy table by hand where an index does the same job

items.explanation: The new query keeps CustomerId as the partition key but needs another sort key, and the table already holds data. You can [add a new global secondary index](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-index-online-operations-gsi-vs-lsi) at any time, and its [index key schema can be different](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-gsi-key-schema-can-differ) from the table. Queries on it [support eventual consistency only](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-index-read-consistency-gsi-vs-lsi), which the screen accepts.
items.takeaway: For a new query on a table that already holds data, add a global secondary index.
items.twin: If the stem said "The table is being created now, and the new screen must use strongly consistent reads." instead: a local secondary index, because it is [created when the table is created](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-lsi-created-with-table).
items.say: The table already has data, so I'd add a GSI with CustomerId and OrderTotal; an LSI can't be added later.

solvers.stem_only: The table already exists, so a local secondary index cannot be added (LSIs are defined only at table creation). Add a GSI with CustomerId as partition key and OrderTotal as sort key; eventually consistent reads from a GSI are acceptable here.

items.stem: A gaming company stores player profiles in an Amazon DynamoDB table. The game reads the same small set of profile items thousands of times each second, and every read is eventually consistent. Reads take a few milliseconds today, and the company wants them to return in microseconds. The company accepts minimal code changes, but it wants no new caching logic in the application. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST development effort?
keywords: same small set of profile items

options.text: Create an Amazon ElastiCache cluster, and add code that reads each profile from the cache first and writes it to the cache after a miss.
options.why: It works, but it adds the cache-aside logic that the company wants to avoid, while DAX needs [only minimal functional changes](../facts/dax.md#dax-api-compatible-minimal-changes) for the same reads.
options.misconception: chooses a general cache that needs new caching code for DynamoDB reads

options.text: Raise the provisioned read capacity of the table to twice the current peak so that each profile read has more capacity to use.
options.why: Capacity sets how many reads the table accepts, not how fast each one returns, and DynamoDB alone gives [single-digit millisecond performance](../facts/dax.md#dax-modest-needs-use-dynamodb-alone).
options.misconception: believes that more read capacity makes each read faster

options.text: Create a DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster for the table, and replace the DynamoDB client in the game with the DAX client.
options.why: DAX is [API-compatible with DynamoDB](../facts/dax.md#dax-api-compatible-minimal-changes) and returns [eventually consistent data](../facts/dax.md#dax-eventually-consistent-microsecond-latency) [with microsecond latency](../facts/dax.md#dax-eventually-consistent-microsecond-latency), so the game changes its client, not its calls.

options.text: Move the player profiles into an Amazon ElastiCache cluster, and delete the DynamoDB table so that every read comes from memory.
options.why: ElastiCache is an [ephemeral cache for frequently accessed data](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-decision-guide-elasticache-caching-layer), so with the table deleted, the profiles lose their durable store.

items.explanation: The reads repeat, are eventually consistent and need microseconds, which is the DAX pattern. DAX fits applications that [read a small number of items more frequently](../facts/dax.md#dax-ideal-fastest-reads-hot-keys) than others. It is [API-compatible with DynamoDB](../facts/dax.md#dax-api-compatible-minimal-changes), so the game keeps its data access calls and swaps the client.
items.takeaway: Repeated eventually consistent DynamoDB reads that need microseconds: add DAX and swap the client.
items.twin: If the stem said "every profile read must be strongly consistent" instead: DAX does not help, because [DAX passes strongly consistent read requests to DynamoDB](../facts/dax.md#dax-passes-through-strong-reads-and-transactions).

solvers.stem_only: Put DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) in front of the table and point the application at the DAX client: an API-compatible, write-through in-memory cache that serves eventually consistent reads in microseconds without the application writing its own cache logic.

items.stem: A company stores product items in an Amazon DynamoDB table in provisioned capacity mode. Every item is 6 KB in size. The application needs to make 100 strongly consistent reads per second and 50 writes per second on these items. None of the writes are part of a transaction. A solutions architect needs to set the provisioned capacity of the table to match this load. How many read capacity units (RCUs) and write capacity units (WCUs) does the table need?

options.text: 100 RCUs and 300 WCUs
options.why: This prices each read like an eventually consistent read, but a unit gives [one strongly consistent read operation per second](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-rcu-definition) per block, so these reads need twice as many units.
options.misconception: prices each strongly consistent read like an eventually consistent read

options.text: 200 RCUs and 50 WCUs
options.why: This counts one unit per write, but a unit covers [one write per second for an item up to 1 KB](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-wcu-definition), so a larger item takes more units.

options.text: 150 RCUs and 300 WCUs
options.why: This divides the item size by the read block without rounding up, but sizes round up to the [next 4 KB multiple](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-read-rounding-4kb) before the division.
options.misconception: divides the item size by the read block without rounding up

options.text: 200 RCUs and 300 WCUs
options.why: A read rounds up to the [next 4 KB multiple](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-read-rounding-4kb), so each strongly consistent read takes two units; each write takes six units, because you [divide the item size of the operation by 1 KB](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-write-capacity-formula).

items.explanation: For reads, you [divide the item size of the operation by 4 KB](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-read-capacity-formula) and round up, so each strongly consistent read takes two units. For writes, you [divide the item size of the operation by 1 KB](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-write-capacity-formula), so each write takes six units. Multiply each by the request rates in the stem.
items.takeaway: Reads round up to the [next 4 KB multiple](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-read-rounding-4kb) and writes to the [next 1 KB multiple](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-write-rounding-1kb); then multiply by the rate.
items.twin: If the stem said "100 eventually consistent reads per second" instead: half the read units, because one RCU gives [two eventually consistent read operations per second](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-rcu-definition).

solvers.stem_only: Strongly consistent read of 6 KB = ceil(6/4) = 2 RCUs, x100 = 200 RCUs. Standard write of 6 KB = 6 WCUs (1 KB units), x50 = 300 WCUs. Answer 200 RCUs and 300 WCUs.

items.stem: A company stores support tickets as items in an Amazon DynamoDB table. Agents update each ticket many times during its life. When the status of a ticket changes to CLOSED, the company must send a satisfaction survey email to the customer in near real-time. The solution must not send a second email when an agent edits a ticket that is already closed. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: status of a ticket changes to CLOSED

options.text: Turn on DynamoDB Streams, and have an AWS Lambda function read the stream records once a week and email every ticket that was closed that week.
options.why: Stream records have a [lifetime of 24 hours](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-stream-records-24-hours), so a weekly job misses most changes, and the emails are days late.

options.text: Run an AWS Lambda function every minute on an Amazon EventBridge schedule that scans the table for closed tickets and emails the ones not yet emailed.
options.why: It works, but each run reads the whole table, because in a Scan [DynamoDB reads every item](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-scan-reads-every-item), and the code tracks the emails it sent.
options.misconception: polls the whole table instead of reacting to each item change

options.text: Turn on DynamoDB Streams with new and old item images, and add an AWS Lambda trigger that emails when the status changes to CLOSED.
options.why: A trigger can [automatically respond to events in DynamoDB Streams](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-streams-lambda-triggers), and the record holds [both the new and the old images](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-streams-view-new-and-old-images), so the function sees the change to CLOSED.

options.text: Turn on DynamoDB Streams, and run an application on Amazon EC2 instances that polls the stream of the table and sends the survey emails.
options.why: It can work, but the team runs, patches and scales instances, while a Lambda trigger needs no servers to manage.
options.misconception: runs its own stream reader on instances where a managed trigger exists

items.explanation: The email follows one item change. DynamoDB Streams records a [time-ordered sequence of every item-level change](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-streams-time-ordered-changes) in [near-real time](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-streams-time-ordered-changes), and a stream has a [native integration with AWS Lambda](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-faq-streams-lambda-triggers). The old image shows whether the ticket was already closed, so an edit of a closed ticket sends no second email.
items.takeaway: Run code on each item change with a stream and a Lambda trigger; keep old images to compare.
items.twin: If the stem said "an audit job must replay every status change of the last 7 days" instead: Kinesis Data Streams for DynamoDB, because it keeps records [up to 1 year](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-streams-vs-kds-retention).

solvers.stem_only: Enable DynamoDB Streams with NEW_AND_OLD_IMAGES and a Lambda trigger (event source mapping) that sends the email only when the old image status is not CLOSED and the new image status is CLOSED.

items.stem: An online store keeps its product catalog in an Amazon DynamoDB table. Product pages read the same popular items thousands of times each second. For the product pages, data that is a few seconds old is acceptable, and reads must return in microseconds. At checkout, the application must read the current price of each item with a strongly consistent read. Which solution meets these requirements in the MOST operationally efficient way?
keywords: a few seconds old is acceptable

options.text: Copy the popular items into the memory of each web server, refresh the copies every few seconds, and read checkout prices from the table.
options.why: It can work, but the team builds and refreshes a cache on every web server, while DAX is managed and [API-compatible with DynamoDB](../facts/dax.md#dax-api-compatible-minimal-changes).
options.misconception: builds a cache by hand on each server where a managed cache exists

options.text: Add a DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster, send all reads through the DAX client, and make every read strongly consistent so that checkout uses the cache too.
options.why: DAX passes a strongly consistent read on, and [it does not cache the results](../facts/dax.md#dax-passes-through-strong-reads-and-transactions), so the product pages lose their microsecond reads.

options.text: Add a DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster for the product pages, and read checkout prices from a global secondary index with strongly consistent reads.
options.why: Strongly consistent reads are [only supported on tables and local secondary indexes](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-strong-reads-only-tables-and-lsi), so a global secondary index cannot return the current price.

options.text: Add a DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster, send all reads through the DAX client, and use eventually consistent reads for pages and strongly consistent reads at checkout.
options.why: DAX serves [eventually consistent data](../facts/dax.md#dax-eventually-consistent-microsecond-latency) [with microsecond latency](../facts/dax.md#dax-eventually-consistent-microsecond-latency) to the pages, and [DAX passes strongly consistent read requests to DynamoDB](../facts/dax.md#dax-passes-through-strong-reads-and-transactions) for checkout.

items.explanation: The deciding phrases are microsecond page reads and strong reads at checkout. The DAX client [directs all of your application's DynamoDB API requests](../facts/dax.md#dax-client-routes-requests-to-cluster) to the cluster. Eventually consistent page reads come from the cache, and [DAX passes strongly consistent read requests to DynamoDB](../facts/dax.md#dax-passes-through-strong-reads-and-transactions), so checkout reads the current price from the table.
items.takeaway: DAX caches eventually consistent reads and passes strongly consistent reads to the table.
items.twin: If the stem said "every read, on the pages and at checkout, must be strongly consistent" instead: DAX adds nothing, because for those reads [it does not cache the results](../facts/dax.md#dax-passes-through-strong-reads-and-transactions).

solvers.stem_only: Put DAX in front of the table and route all reads through the DAX client: eventually consistent page reads are served from the DAX item cache in microseconds; strongly consistent checkout reads are passed through by DAX to DynamoDB (not cached).

items.stem: A company will open ticket sales for a large concert at a fixed time next week. The tickets are stored in a new Amazon DynamoDB table in on-demand capacity mode, and the table has served only light test traffic so far. At the opening minute, the company expects a peak of many times more requests than the table has ever served. The company has stringent requirements: no request can be throttled. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: has served only light test traffic

options.text: Before the sale, raise the warm throughput of the table to the expected peak so that the table can serve that rate at once.
options.why: [Pre-warming](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-warm-throughput-prewarm-for-peak-events) raises warm throughput ahead of time and sets a [baseline that your tables can instantly support](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-warm-throughput-prewarm-for-peak-events), so the opening peak is served.

options.text: Keep the table in on-demand capacity mode without other changes, because on-demand capacity mode serves any number of requests the moment they arrive.
options.why: On-demand mode [instantly accommodates up to double the previous peak](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-on-demand-previous-peak-double); above that, [throttling can occur](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-on-demand-throttle-if-double-within-30-min), and this jump is far larger.

options.text: Switch the table to provisioned capacity mode with auto scaling at a 70% target utilization, and let auto scaling add capacity during the sale.
options.why: Auto scaling [does not respond instantly](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-throttling-with-autoscaling-possible), so requests in the opening minute are throttled before the new capacity arrives.

options.text: Run a load script in the days before the sale that sends test traffic which keeps doubling until the table has served the expected peak.
options.why: It can work, because the table then has a higher previous peak, but the team runs load tests for days instead of changing one table setting.
options.misconception: raises the previous peak by hand with synthetic traffic

items.explanation: The table has served only light traffic, and on-demand mode [instantly accommodates up to double the previous peak](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-on-demand-previous-peak-double). Warm throughput is what a table [can instantaneously support](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-warm-throughput-definition). Raising it before the sale, called [pre-warming](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-warm-throughput-prewarm-for-peak-events), prepares the table for the known peak with one change.
items.takeaway: A known launch far above any earlier peak: pre-warm the table by raising its warm throughput.
items.twin: If the stem said "a peak about the same as the busiest day the table has already served" instead: keep on-demand mode, because it [instantly accommodates up to double the previous peak](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-on-demand-previous-peak-double).

solvers.stem_only: Pre-warm the on-demand table by setting its warm throughput (read and write units per second) to the expected peak before the sale, so it can serve that rate immediately without throttling.

items.stem: A company runs a profile service for users around the world. The service stores user profiles in an Amazon DynamoDB table in us-east-1. Users in Europe and Asia report slow saves, because every write travels to us-east-1. Each write must be served in the user's own Region, and the service must stay highly available if one Region fails. Which solution provides the LOWEST latency for writes from every user?
keywords: served in the user's own Region

options.text: Convert the table into a global table, send every write to the replica table in us-east-1, and fail writes over to another Region in an outage.
options.why: It keeps the slow writes: a global table has [no primary Region](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-faq-global-tables-no-failover-needed), yet every write from Europe and Asia still travels to us-east-1.

options.text: Migrate the profiles to an Amazon Aurora global database with a cluster in each user Region, and send each write to the cluster in that Region.
options.why: In an Aurora global database, [only the primary cluster performs write operations](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-vs-aurora-global-database-single-writer), so every write from Europe and Asia still travels to the primary cluster's Region.

options.text: Convert the table into a global table with replica tables in the Regions of the users, and have each Region write to its local replica table.
options.why: [Any global table replica](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-global-table-any-replica-serves-reads-writes) can [serve reads and writes](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-global-table-any-replica-serves-reads-writes), so each user writes to a nearby replica table with [fast local read and write performance](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-global-tables-definition).

options.text: Create DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) clusters in Europe and in Asia that cache the table and accept the profile writes of local users.
options.why: A DAX cluster works only with [tables that are in the same Region](../facts/dax.md#dax-same-region-as-tables), so clusters in Europe and Asia cannot serve a table in us-east-1.
options.misconception: believes that a cache in another Region can take writes for the table

items.explanation: The deciding phrase is local writes in every Region. Global tables are a [multi-Region, and multi-active database](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-faq-global-tables-multi-active), so every replica table accepts writes near its users. If one Region fails, the others keep serving reads and writes, because a global table has [no primary Region](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-faq-global-tables-no-failover-needed).
items.takeaway: Local writes in many Regions: a DynamoDB global table, where every replica table accepts writes.
items.twin: If the stem said "users in Europe and Asia only read profiles, and the data is relational" instead: an Aurora global database, with [up to 10 read-only secondary AWS Regions](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-vs-aurora-global-database-single-writer) for local reads.

solvers.stem_only: DynamoDB global tables (multi-active): add replica tables in the users' Regions, write locally in each Region, replication across Regions; survives a Regional failure.

items.stem: A company stores the order data of its online store in an Amazon DynamoDB table. The table uses provisioned capacity mode with auto scaling. Traffic is unpredictable: the table sits idle for hours, then spikes to earlier peak levels within minutes. The company wants to keep requests from being throttled and wants to lower the monthly cost of the table. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?
keywords: the table sits idle for hours

options.text: Change the table to on-demand capacity mode, so that DynamoDB bills each read and write request that the application makes.
options.why: [On-demand capacity mode is the better choice](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-ondemand-better-for-fluctuating-traffic) for spiky traffic, and a table [billed per read or write request](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-ondemand-billed-per-request-zero-traffic-free) pays no throughput charge in idle hours.

options.text: Keep provisioned capacity mode with auto scaling, and purchase reserved capacity for the base level of reads and writes of the table.
options.why: Reserved capacity lowers the base price, but auto scaling [does not respond instantly](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-throttling-with-autoscaling-possible), so sudden spikes are still throttled.

options.text: Keep provisioned capacity mode with auto scaling, and add a DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster in front of the table for all requests.
options.why: With DAX, data is [first written to the DynamoDB table](../facts/dax.md#dax-write-through-both-table-and-dax), so the cluster adds cost and the write spikes still reach the table.

options.text: Keep provisioned capacity mode, turn off auto scaling, and set the read and write capacity to the highest level that the table has used.
options.why: Capacity at the peak stops the throttling, but the company pays for the [hourly read and write capacity you have provisioned](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-provisioned-billing-basis) in every idle hour.
options.misconception: Provisioning the highest peak around the clock is a cost-effective way to stop throttling.

items.explanation: For traffic that is idle for hours and then spikes, [on-demand capacity mode is the better choice](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-ondemand-better-for-fluctuating-traffic). The table is [billed per read or write request](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-ondemand-billed-per-request-zero-traffic-free), so the idle hours cost no throughput. In provisioned mode, auto scaling [does not respond instantly](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-throttling-with-autoscaling-possible) to a sudden spike.
items.takeaway: Spiky, unpredictable DynamoDB traffic with idle hours: on-demand capacity mode, billed per request.
items.twin: If the stem said "Traffic is steady-state and predictable: the table uses almost all of its provisioned capacity around the clock." instead: provisioned mode with reserved capacity, because it fits a [more steady and predictable usage pattern](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-provisioned-ideal-steady-predictable-usage).
items.say: Spiky traffic with idle hours points to on-demand mode, because it bills per request and needs no capacity plan.

solvers.stem_only: Spiky, unpredictable traffic with long idle periods: switch to on-demand capacity mode, paying per request with no idle capacity and no auto scaling lag.

items.stem: A company stores customer orders in an Amazon DynamoDB table. Point-in-time recovery is turned on with its default settings, and an on-demand backup of the table is taken every Sunday. The table also has a DynamoDB stream that a search service reads. On Tuesday at 14:05, a faulty release deleted thousands of order items. The team found the problem on Friday. The company must get the deleted items back as they were at 14:04, a point in time before the error. What should a solutions architect do?
keywords: The team found the problem on Friday

options.text: Restore the table to Tuesday at 14:04 directly into the existing table, so that the production table rolls back in place.
options.why: You [can't overwrite an existing table](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-restore-cannot-overwrite-existing-table) during a restore, so no restore rolls the production table back in place.

options.text: Restore the Sunday on-demand backup to a new table, and copy the deleted items from the new table into the production table.
options.why: The Sunday backup misses the orders that were created or changed between Sunday and Tuesday, so the items do not come back as they were at 14:04.
options.misconception: The latest scheduled backup is good enough for a recovery to an exact time.

options.text: Read the old images of the deleted items from the DynamoDB stream of the table, and write the items back into the production table.
options.why: Stream records have a [lifetime of 24 hours](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-stream-records-24-hours), so the records of the Tuesday deletes were removed from the stream before Friday.

options.text: Restore the table to Tuesday at 14:04 as a new table, and copy the deleted items from the new table into the production table.
options.why: Point-in-time recovery [always restores to a new table](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-pitr-restores-to-new-table), and copying the deleted items back returns them as they were at 14:04.

items.explanation: Point-in-time recovery protects a table [from accidental write or delete operations](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-pitr-protects-accidental-writes-deletes). The process [always restores to a new table](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-pitr-restores-to-new-table), because you [can't overwrite an existing table](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-restore-cannot-overwrite-existing-table) during a restore. The team restores to 14:04 and copies the deleted items back into production.
items.takeaway: A DynamoDB point-in-time restore creates a new table; copy the items back or switch the application to it.
items.twin: If the stem said "a faulty release deleted the whole table" instead: restore the [system backup](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-pitr-deleted-table-system-backup) that DynamoDB creates when a table with point-in-time recovery is deleted.
items.say: Point-in-time recovery restores into a new table, so I restore to 14:04 and copy the deleted items back.

solvers.stem_only: PITR (default 35-day recovery window) covers Tuesday 14:04; a PITR restore always creates a new table, so restore to 14:04 into a new table and copy the deleted items back. Stream records expire after 24 hours, and the Sunday backup is not the 14:04 state.

items.stem: A startup with a small team is building a serverless backend for a mobile app. AWS Lambda functions handle every request. Each request reads or writes one user session by its session ID, and no request joins session data with other data. Traffic swings from almost nothing at night to millions of requests at peak. Session data must be stored durably. Which database solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: reads or writes one user session by its session ID
Session data must be stored durably

options.text: Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL in a Multi-AZ deployment, with each Lambda invocation opening its own database connection
options.why: Unlike RDS, [DynamoDB uses an HTTP API](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-ddb-http-api-no-connections); a connection per invocation at peak needs pooling, and the team still sizes DB instances.

options.text: Amazon DynamoDB in on-demand capacity mode, with the session ID as the partition key of the session table
options.why: DynamoDB fits [session stores or shopping carts](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-decision-guide-key-value-session-store), and you [don't need to provision any servers](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-serverless-no-servers); on-demand mode can [handle fluctuating traffic](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-ondemand-better-for-fluctuating-traffic).

options.text: A self-managed NoSQL database on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group across three Availability Zones
options.why: DynamoDB, instead of a self-hosted NoSQL database, [can reduce operational overhead](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-wa-managed-nosql-reduces-overhead); here the team patches and scales the instances.
options.misconception: A NoSQL database on your own instances costs the team about the same effort as a managed one.

options.text: A node-based Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached cluster as the only store of session data, keyed by session ID
options.why: Memcached [node-based clusters do not support replication](../facts/elasticache.md#elasticache-memcached-node-based-no-replication-data-loss), so a node failure [will always result in some data loss](../facts/elasticache.md#elasticache-memcached-node-based-no-replication-data-loss), which fails the need to store sessions durably.

items.explanation: Each request reads one item by its key, with no joins, which fits a key-value database for [session stores or shopping carts](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-decision-guide-key-value-session-store). With DynamoDB you [don't need to provision any servers](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-serverless-no-servers). Lambda calls it without connection pools, because [DynamoDB uses an HTTP API](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-ddb-http-api-no-connections).
items.takeaway: Key-value sessions, spiky traffic and a small team: DynamoDB in on-demand mode.
items.twin: If the stem said "the app joins sessions with orders in ad hoc SQL reports" instead: a relational database such as Amazon Aurora, because DynamoDB [doesn't support a JOIN operator](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-no-join-operator).
items.say: One session per key, no joins and spiky traffic point to DynamoDB in on-demand mode, with no servers to manage.

solvers.stem_only: Amazon DynamoDB in on-demand capacity mode with session ID as the partition key: serverless, durable, key-value access, scales from near zero to millions of requests without capacity planning, and no connection management problem with Lambda.

items.stem: A company runs a loyalty program that stores the points balance of each user as an item in an Amazon DynamoDB table. A transfer moves points from one user to another. The transfer is transactional: the debit of one item and the credit of the other item must both succeed or both fail, and the debit must fail if the balance is too low. Clients sometimes time out and send the same transfer request again. The company must ensure that no transfer is applied twice. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST development effort?
keywords: must both succeed or both fail
send the same transfer request again

options.text: Send one BatchWriteItem request that holds both balance changes, and send the same request again when the client times out.
options.why: With BatchWriteItem, [only some of the actions](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-transactwriteitems-vs-batchwriteitem) might succeed, so a debit can be written without its credit.

options.text: Send two UpdateItem requests that change the balances with atomic counters, and retry each request when the client times out.
options.why: With atomic counters, [the updates are not idempotent](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-atomic-counter-not-idempotent): each retry moves the points again, and the two requests can succeed separately.
options.misconception: An atomic counter update can be retried safely.

options.text: Send two conditional UpdateItem requests, store each request ID in a second table, and write code that reverses a failed transfer.
options.why: This design can work, but the team writes and maintains rollback code and duplicate checks that a transaction already provides.
options.misconception: Custom rollback code is the normal way to make two writes succeed or fail together.

options.text: Send one TransactWriteItems request with both updates, a condition on the balance, and a client request token for each transfer.
options.why: TransactWriteItems gives a [guaranteed all-or-nothing result](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-transactwriteitems-all-or-nothing), and the request can [include a client token](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-transactwriteitems-idempotent-client-token) so that a repeated request is not applied twice.

items.explanation: One TransactWriteItems request makes both updates with a [guaranteed all-or-nothing result](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-transactwriteitems-all-or-nothing). A condition on the balance stops a debit that is too large, because [a conditional write succeeds](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-conditional-write-succeeds-only-if-condition) only if its condition is met. The client can [include a client token](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-transactwriteitems-idempotent-client-token) to make a retried request idempotent.
items.takeaway: Two items that change together, with safe retries: TransactWriteItems with conditions and a client token.
items.twin: If the stem said "a client can repeat a request an hour later" instead: also store each request ID and check it in the transaction, because a client token is valid for [10 minutes](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-transaction-client-token-10-minutes).
items.say: Both writes succeed or fail together, so I use TransactWriteItems with a condition and a client token for retries.

solvers.stem_only: One TransactWriteItems call with both updates and a condition expression on the debit (balance >= amount), plus a ClientRequestToken per transfer so a retried request is idempotent.

items.stem: A company is building a reporting service for its sales team. Every week, analysts write new ad hoc SQL queries that join orders, customers, and products, and the access patterns are not known in advance. The data is relational and changes all day as new orders arrive. The team has two developers and no database administrator. Which database solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: new ad hoc SQL queries that join orders, customers, and products
the access patterns are not known in advance

options.text: Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL, with the orders, customers, and products in related tables that the analysts query with SQL
options.why: Aurora fits [less predictable query patterns](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-decision-guide-aurora-relational-joins), and relational databases support [complex queries through joins](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-decision-guide-aurora-relational-joins).

options.text: Amazon DynamoDB, with one table for each entity and a global secondary index for each report that the analysts need
options.why: DynamoDB [doesn't support a JOIN operator](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-no-join-operator), and NoSQL data is [queried efficiently in a limited number of ways](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-nosql-queries-efficient-in-limited-ways), not by new ad hoc queries.

options.text: Amazon ElastiCache, as the fully managed in-memory store that holds the orders, customers, and products for the reports
options.why: ElastiCache is an [ephemeral cache for frequently accessed data](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-decision-guide-elasticache-caching-layer), a layer in front of a database, so it is not the store of record for the reports.

options.text: PostgreSQL on Amazon EC2 instances that the developers install, patch, back up, and scale for the SQL queries of the analysts
options.why: PostgreSQL on EC2 runs the joins, but the two developers patch, back up, and scale the instances themselves.
options.misconception: A database on your own instances gives the same result with the same effort as a managed one.

items.explanation: The analysts write new joins every week, so the access patterns are not known in advance. The AWS decision guide points to Aurora for [less predictable query patterns](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-decision-guide-aurora-relational-joins). Aurora is a [fully managed relational database engine](../facts/aurora.md#aurora-is-managed-relational-engine), so the two developers do not run database instances themselves.
items.takeaway: Ad hoc SQL with joins and unknown access patterns: a relational engine such as Aurora, not DynamoDB.
items.twin: If the stem said "every request reads one order by its order ID, with no joins" instead: Amazon DynamoDB, because for that access AWS says to [consider a NoSQL database such as DynamoDB](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-wa-oltp-dynamodb-vs-rds-joins).
items.say: New joins every week mean unknown access patterns, so I choose Aurora, not DynamoDB.

solvers.stem_only: A managed relational database with SQL joins and ad hoc queries: Amazon Aurora (PostgreSQL or MySQL) or Amazon RDS; not DynamoDB, which needs known access patterns.

items.stem: A web application stores user sessions in an Amazon DynamoDB table that holds millions of items. The application reads each session by its session ID. Each session must expire one hour after its last use, and the application must never accept an expired session. Old session items must be removed from the table automatically. Which TWO actions will meet these requirements in the MOST operationally efficient way? (Select TWO.)
keywords: must never accept an expired session

options.text: Store the expiry time of each session as a Number in Unix epoch seconds, and enable Time to Live on that attribute.
options.why: The TTL attribute uses [Unix epoch time format at the seconds granularity](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-ttl-attribute-number-epoch-seconds), and TTL deletes items [without consuming any write throughput](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-faq-ttl-no-write-throughput).

options.text: Enable Time to Live on the expiry attribute, and accept every session item that a read returns, because expired items are gone.
options.why: DynamoDB deletes expired items [within a few days of their expiration time](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-ttl-deletes-within-days-no-wcu), so a read can still return an expired session.

options.text: In every session read, compare the stored expiry time with the current time, and reject any session item that has expired.
options.why: Expired items [continue to show in read and write operations](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-ttl-expired-items-visible-until-deleted) until deletion, so the application checks the expiry time on every read.

options.text: Store the expiry time of each session as an ISO 8601 date string, and enable Time to Live on that attribute.
options.why: Items whose TTL attribute is not a Number are [ignored by the TTL process](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-ttl-non-number-attribute-ignored), so the sessions stay in the table.
options.misconception: Time to Live reads any date format.

options.text: Run a Lambda function every minute on an Amazon EventBridge schedule that scans the table and deletes expired session items.
options.why: The job works, but the team maintains code, and its scans and deletes use capacity; TTL deletes [without consuming any write throughput](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-faq-ttl-no-write-throughput).
options.misconception: A scheduled clean-up job is the standard way to expire DynamoDB items.

items.explanation: TTL removes old sessions without code: the expiry is a Number in [Unix epoch time format at the seconds granularity](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-ttl-attribute-number-epoch-seconds), and the deletes run [without consuming any write throughput](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-faq-ttl-no-write-throughput). TTL is not exact: items go [within a few days of their expiration time](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-ttl-deletes-within-days-no-wcu), so every read also rejects an expired session.
items.takeaway: TTL deletes expired items within days, not at once; reject expired items in every read.
items.twin: If the stem said "an expired session can be accepted for a few days" instead: TTL alone is enough, because DynamoDB deletes items [within a few days of their expiration time](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-ttl-deletes-within-days-no-wcu).
items.say: TTL cleans up expired sessions without write cost, but late, so the application still checks the expiry time on every read.

solvers.stem_only: Store the expiry as a Number in Unix epoch seconds and enable TTL on that attribute for automatic deletion; because TTL deletes expired items lazily (typically within a few days), the application must also check the expiry time on each read and reject expired sessions (or filter them out).

items.stem: A company runs its order service in us-east-1 and stores the orders in an Amazon DynamoDB table in on-demand capacity mode in the same Region. The company is planning cross-Region disaster recovery for a failure of the whole Region. If us-east-1 fails, users must keep reading and writing orders in us-west-2 immediately, with no restore step. Which solution meets these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?
keywords: keep reading and writing orders in us-west-2 immediately

options.text: Convert the table into a global table, and add a replica table in us-west-2 that the application can read from and write to.
options.why: [Any global table replica](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-global-table-any-replica-serves-reads-writes) can [serve reads and writes](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-global-table-any-replica-serves-reads-writes), and a global table gives an [RTO of zero](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-dr-global-tables-mrec-rto-zero), so us-west-2 takes the orders at once.

options.text: Use AWS Backup to back up the table every hour, and copy each backup to a backup vault in us-west-2 for restores.
options.why: A backup is restored into a new table before anyone can use it, and hourly copies give an [RPO of 1 hour](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-dr-aws-backup-rpo-1-hour), not writes in us-west-2 at once.

options.text: Convert the table into a global table, and add replica tables in us-west-2 and in eu-west-1 that the application can read from and write to.
options.why: It works, but the eu-west-1 replica table adds a replicated write request unit (rWRU) charge, [one rWRU per replica table](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-gt-rwru-per-replica) for every write, which no requirement needs.

options.text: Create a DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster in us-west-2 that caches the items of the table and serves them to the application during an outage.
options.why: A DAX cluster can work only with [tables that are in the same Region](../facts/dax.md#dax-same-region-as-tables), so a cluster in us-west-2 cannot serve this table.
options.misconception: believes that a cache in another Region can stand in for the table

items.explanation: Users need to write in us-west-2 at once, with no restore step. A global table has [no primary Region](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-faq-global-tables-no-failover-needed), so no database failover is needed, and replication gives an [RPO of a few seconds](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-dr-global-tables-mrec-rto-zero). One replica table in us-west-2 meets the need at the lowest cost.
items.takeaway: Reads and writes in a second Region at once: a global table with one replica table there.
items.twin: If the stem said "If us-east-1 fails, a restore in us-west-2 within hours is acceptable, and so is losing up to 1 hour of data." instead: AWS Backup with hourly copies, for an [RPO of 1 hour](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-dr-aws-backup-rpo-1-hour).

solvers.stem_only: Convert to a global table with one replica table in us-west-2 (active-active, no restore step); one extra Region is the cheapest design that meets the requirement.

items.stem: A company runs a voting application that stores each vote as an item in an Amazon DynamoDB table in provisioned capacity mode. The partition key is the contest ID, and the application shows the running total of each contest. During a televised final, almost every vote is for one contest, at about 4,000 votes each second. Each vote item is smaller than 1 KB. Amazon CloudWatch shows that consumed write capacity is far below the provisioned write capacity of the table, but many writes are throttled. The company needs a scalable design. Which solution will BEST resolve the throttling?
keywords: almost every vote is for one contest
far below the provisioned write capacity

options.text: Raise the provisioned write capacity of the table to several times the current peak, and keep the contest ID as the partition key of every vote.
options.why: The table already has spare capacity; the limit is one partition, which delivers at most [1,000 write units per second](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-partition-max-throughput) whatever the table total is.

options.text: Add a random number from a fixed range to the contest ID on each write, then query each suffix and sum the results to count the votes.
options.why: Random suffixes [randomize the writes across the larger space](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-write-sharding-random-suffix) of keys, and a total needs one query per suffix before you [merge the results](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-write-sharding-read-merge).

options.text: Switch the table to on-demand capacity mode so that the table scales automatically with the burst of votes, and keep the contest ID as the partition key.
options.why: On-demand mode changes billing, not the partition ceiling of [1,000 write units per second](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-partition-max-throughput), so 4,000 small votes each second on one key are still throttled.

options.text: Make a unique vote ID the partition key of every item, and count the votes of a contest with a Scan that filters on the contest ID.
options.why: It ends the throttling, but in a Scan [DynamoDB reads every item](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-scan-reads-every-item), so each running total reads the whole table.
options.misconception: fixes the writes with a design that makes every total a full table read

items.explanation: Consumed capacity is far below provisioned capacity, so the table is not short of capacity; one partition key is. A partition delivers at most [1,000 write units per second](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-partition-max-throughput), and [concentrated traffic that exceeds these limits](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-hot-partitions-throttle-while-others-underutilized) is throttled. Write sharding spreads one contest [across more distinct partition key values](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-few-partition-keys-spread-writes), so no single partition takes the whole burst.
items.takeaway: Throttling with spare table capacity means a hot partition key: spread it with a random suffix.
items.twin: If the stem said "consumed write capacity equals the provisioned write capacity, and the votes are spread across many contests" instead: raise the provisioned write capacity, because the table as a whole is short of capacity.
items.say: Spare capacity plus throttling means one hot key, so I'd shard the key with a random suffix.

steps: I read the last sentence first: it asks for the solution that BEST resolves the throttling.

I mark the constraints: almost every vote is for one contest at about 4,000 small writes each second, the contest ID is the partition key, consumed write capacity is far below the provisioned capacity, and the application shows a running total per contest.
Before I look at the options, I predict a change of the partition key, because throttling with spare table capacity points to one hot key, and a random suffix spreads that key.

I remove the higher provisioned capacity, because the table already has spare capacity and each partition has its own ceiling. I remove on-demand mode, because it changes billing, not the ceiling of one partition.

Between the random suffix and the unique vote ID the difference is how the totals are read; the stem needs a running total per contest, so a Scan of the whole table for each total is the weaker design.
Check: the random suffix spreads the writes, a total needs one query per suffix, and every constraint is met. Time: 90 seconds.

solvers.flag: Minor stem gap: the stem never says the table has a sort key (for example a vote ID), yet with contest ID as the only key each vote would overwrite the previous item; stating the sort key would remove the doubt, and it does not change the key.
solvers.stem_only: This is a hot partition key: one contest ID takes almost all writes, so a single partition hits its per-partition write limit while table-level capacity is unused. Fix the key design with write sharding: append a random suffix from a fixed range to the contest ID so writes spread over many partitions, then read all suffixes and sum for the total.

solvers.flag: The stem does not say whether the table has a sort key, and a careful candidate could defend C (on-demand mode, which can also isolate hot items by splitting partitions) if the votes have a sort key; adding a line that the single contest ID value receives all traffic and that a single partition key value is capped would remove the doubt.

items.stem: An online store uses Amazon DynamoDB for its orders table. The partition key of the table is CustomerId, and the sort key is OrderDate. A new screen in the application must list the orders of one customer sorted by OrderTotal. The table is being created now, and the new screen must use strongly consistent reads. The table will grow to millions of orders, and the screen must stay fast as the table grows. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: must stay fast as the table grows

options.text: Add a global secondary index with CustomerId as the partition key and OrderTotal as the sort key, and query the index for the screen.
options.why: The screen needs strongly consistent reads, but queries on a global secondary index [support eventual consistency only](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-index-read-consistency-gsi-vs-lsi).

options.text: Define a local secondary index on the table with OrderTotal as the sort key, and query the index for the screen.
options.why: The table is new, so the index is [created when the table is created](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-lsi-created-with-table), and a query can use [either eventually consistent or strongly consistent reads](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-lsi-strongly-consistent-allowed).

options.text: Scan the table with a filter expression on CustomerId for each request, and sort the returned orders by OrderTotal in the application.
options.why: It needs no index, but a Scan [always scans the entire table or secondary index](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-scan-less-efficient-than-query), and it slows [as a table or index grows](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-scan-slows-as-table-grows), so the screen does not stay fast.

options.text: Copy each order into a second table keyed by CustomerId and OrderTotal through a Lambda function that reads the stream of the table.
options.why: The copy is written from the stream after each change, and [reads from GSIs and streams are eventually consistent](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-gsi-and-streams-reads-eventual), so the copy can miss the latest write.
options.misconception: treats a copy that is written after each change as current

items.explanation: The screen needs strong reads on another sort key of the same customer. A local secondary index has the [same partition key as the base table](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-lsi-same-partition-key) and its own sort key. Strongly consistent reads are [only supported on tables and local secondary indexes](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-strong-reads-only-tables-and-lsi), and the table is new, so the index can be defined now.
items.takeaway: Strong reads on another sort key of a new table: define a local secondary index at creation.
items.twin: If the stem said "The table currently holds two years of orders, and eventually consistent reads are acceptable." instead: a global secondary index, because you can [add a new global secondary index](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-index-online-operations-gsi-vs-lsi) later.

solvers.stem_only: Same partition key (CustomerId), different sort key (OrderTotal), strongly consistent reads, table not yet created: a local secondary index defined at table creation with OrderTotal as its sort key; query it per customer. A GSI cannot serve strongly consistent reads.

items.stem: A company runs an order application that writes each new order to an Amazon DynamoDB table with a PutItem request. Right after each write, the application reads the same order back with a GetItem request to show a confirmation page. Sometimes the confirmation page shows the previous version of the order. Every read-back must return the result of all earlier successful writes. What should a solutions architect do?
keywords: shows the previous version of the order
must return the result of all earlier successful writes

options.text: Read the order back from a global secondary index on the order ID, with a strongly consistent query on the index.
options.why: Queries on a global secondary index [support eventual consistency only](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-index-read-consistency-gsi-vs-lsi), so a strongly consistent query on the index is not possible.

options.text: Add a DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster, and send only the GetItem read-back requests through the DAX client.
options.why: DAX serves [eventually consistent data](../facts/dax.md#dax-eventually-consistent-microsecond-latency), and writes that bypass DAX leave the cache to [hold inconsistent values for the same key](../facts/dax.md#dax-bypass-causes-inconsistent-values).
options.misconception: A read from an in-memory cache returns the newest write.

options.text: Set the ConsistentRead parameter to true on the GetItem request that the application sends after each write.
options.why: With ConsistentRead set to true, GetItem returns the [most up-to-date data](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-consistentread-parameter), which reflects every earlier successful write.

options.text: Enable DynamoDB Streams on the table, and read the newest version of the order from the stream after the write.
options.why: A stream serves other consumers of changes, and [reads from GSIs and streams are eventually consistent](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-gsi-and-streams-reads-eventual), so the read can still miss the write.
options.misconception: A DynamoDB stream returns the newest committed version of an item.

items.explanation: [Eventually consistent is the default](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-eventually-consistent-default) for reads, and such a read [might not reflect the results](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-eventually-consistent-may-lag) of a recent write. A GetItem request with ConsistentRead set to true returns the [most up-to-date data](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-consistentread-parameter).
items.takeaway: To read your own write in DynamoDB, set ConsistentRead to true on the table read.
items.twin: If the stem said "the page can show an order that is a few seconds old" instead: keep the default eventually consistent read, at [half the cost of strongly consistent reads](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-eventually-consistent-half-cost).
items.say: A read right after a write needs ConsistentRead set to true, because the default read is eventually consistent.

solvers.stem_only: Use a strongly consistent read: set ConsistentRead=true on the GetItem read-back.

items.stem: A company runs a mission-critical order API on an Amazon DynamoDB table in provisioned capacity mode. Every night, a report job scans the whole table with strongly consistent reads and a filter expression that keeps only orders with the status OPEN. A small share of the orders are open at any time, and the report can use data that is a few minutes old. The company wants no new tables or functions to operate. During the job, the order API is throttled. Which TWO actions will reduce the read capacity that the job consumes in the MOST cost-effective way? (Select TWO.)
keywords: a filter expression that keeps only orders with the status OPEN
A small share of the orders are open
the report can use data that is a few minutes old

options.text: Make the filter expression of the scan more selective, so that the scan returns fewer order items to the report job.
options.why: A filter runs after the read, so the scan [consumes the same amount of read capacity](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-scan-filter-same-read-capacity) with or without it.

options.text: Add an attribute that only open orders carry, create a global secondary index on that attribute, and change the job to query the index.
options.why: The index [only tracks data items](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-gsi-only-items-with-key-attributes) that carry its key, so it is [faster and less expensive to query that index](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-sparse-index-faster-cheaper-than-scan).

options.text: Add a projection expression to the scan, so that DynamoDB returns only the few attributes that the report needs.
options.why: Read capacity depends on [the number of items and the size](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-read-capacity-by-items-read-not-returned) of the items that the scan reads, not on the data it returns.

options.text: Change the scan of the report job from strongly consistent reads to eventually consistent reads, and keep the same filter expression.
options.why: Eventually consistent reads cost [half the cost of strongly consistent reads](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-eventually-consistent-half-cost), and the report accepts data that is minutes old.

options.text: Copy each open order into a second DynamoDB table with a Lambda function on the stream of the table, and scan the second table.
options.why: It adds a second table and a Lambda function, which the company does not want to operate, and it also pays for every copied write.
options.misconception: A copy that custom code keeps in sync is the cheapest way to isolate a report.

items.explanation: A filter does not help, because the scan still [consumes the same amount of read capacity](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-scan-filter-same-read-capacity). A sparse global secondary index [only tracks data items](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-gsi-only-items-with-key-attributes) that carry its key attribute, so the job reads far fewer items. Eventually consistent reads then cost [half the cost of strongly consistent reads](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-eventually-consistent-half-cost).
items.takeaway: Filters and projections do not lower scan capacity; a sparse index and eventually consistent reads do.
items.twin: If the stem said "the report lists every order, open or closed" instead: the sparse index stops helping, because the job reads every item, and eventually consistent reads still help.
items.say: To cut the read capacity of a report, I query a sparse index and use eventually consistent reads; a filter saves nothing.

solvers.stem_only: A scan is charged for every item it reads before filters and projections apply, so filters and projections do not help. Reduce consumed capacity by (1) switching the scan to eventually consistent reads, which costs half as much, since stale data is acceptable, and (2) replacing the full scan with a query on a sparse global secondary index keyed on an attribute that only open orders carry.
