solvers.flag: A and C are alternatives rather than a complementary pair (once the job queries a sparse index, the eventually consistent setting of the old scan no longer applies; the GSI query is eventually consistent by nature), and A needs a write-path change plus a backfill and adds index write cost, so a candidate could defend 'C plus one of B or D' only if they wrongly think filters or projections cut scan read capacity; the stem should make clear that exactly two independent savings are meant.

items.stem: A company keeps 5 years of order history in an Amazon DynamoDB table that uses the DynamoDB Standard table class. The company must retain all of the orders, and the application reads old orders through the same DynamoDB API as new orders. Orders older than one month are infrequently accessed. Storage is about 70% of the monthly bill of the table. The company does not want to change the application code. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?
keywords: must retain all of the orders
Storage is about 70% of the monthly bill

options.text: Enable Time to Live on the order table so that DynamoDB deletes each order item one month after the order date.
options.why: Deleting old orders lowers the bill, but it breaks the requirement to retain all of the orders.

options.text: Export the orders older than one month to Amazon S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval, and delete those orders from the table.
options.why: Archived orders leave the table, so the application can no longer read them through the same DynamoDB API.

options.text: Change the table class of the order table from DynamoDB Standard to the DynamoDB Standard-Infrequent Access (DynamoDB Standard-IA) table class.
options.why: Standard-IA has [lower storage costs than DynamoDB Standard](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-table-class-standard-ia-lower-storage-cost), and the switch [does not require changing your application code](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-table-class-switch-no-code-change).

options.text: Keep the DynamoDB Standard table class, and purchase reserved capacity for the reads and writes that the table uses each month.
options.why: Reserved capacity discounts only reads and writes, but here [storage is the dominant cost](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-table-class-standard-ia-lower-storage-cost), and Standard-IA lowers it.
options.misconception: A commitment discount on throughput is the biggest saving for every table.

items.explanation: Storage is about 70% of the bill, and DynamoDB Standard-IA suits tables whose storage is [approximately 50% or more of the overall monthly cost](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-table-class-standard-vs-ia-50-percent-storage). It offers the [same performance, durability, and availability](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-table-class-standard-ia-same-performance) as Standard, and the switch [does not require changing your application code](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-table-class-switch-no-code-change).
items.takeaway: When storage is half or more of a DynamoDB bill, switch the table class to Standard-IA.
items.twin: If the stem said "Storage is about 20% of the monthly bill" instead: keep DynamoDB Standard, which suits tables whose storage is [approximately 50% or less of the overall monthly cost](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-table-class-standard-vs-ia-50-percent-storage).
items.say: Storage is most of the bill and old orders are rarely read, so I switch the table to Standard-IA, with no code change.

solvers.stem_only: Change the table class to DynamoDB Standard-IA: lower storage price for storage-dominated, infrequently accessed tables, same API, no code change.

items.stem: A company runs applications in private subnets of a VPC and servers in its on-premises data center. The data center connects to the VPC through AWS Direct Connect. Both the applications and the servers read and write items in an Amazon DynamoDB table in the same Region. The applications exchange several terabytes of data with DynamoDB each day; the servers exchange much less. All traffic to DynamoDB must reach the service privately, without using the public internet. Which TWO actions will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way? (Select TWO.)
keywords: servers in its on-premises data center

options.text: Create a NAT gateway in each Availability Zone, and route the DynamoDB traffic of the private subnets through the NAT gateways.
options.why: A gateway endpoint reaches DynamoDB [without requiring an internet gateway or NAT device](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-faq-gateway-endpoint-no-igw-nat), and NAT gateways charge per gigabyte [regardless of the traffic's source or destination](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-data-processing-any-destination).
options.misconception: Private subnets need a NAT gateway to reach DynamoDB.

options.text: Create a gateway endpoint for DynamoDB, and add the endpoint to the route tables of the private subnets of the applications.
options.why: A gateway endpoint reaches DynamoDB [without requiring an internet gateway or NAT device](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-faq-gateway-endpoint-no-igw-nat), and there is [no additional charge for using gateway endpoints](../facts/vpc-endpoints.md#vpc-endpoints-wp-gateway-endpoint-no-additional-charge).

options.text: Route the requests of the data center servers over Direct Connect to the gateway endpoint that the private subnets use.
options.why: Gateway endpoints do not allow access from on-premises networks; for that case [you must use AWS PrivateLink](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-faq-gateway-endpoint-limits-use-privatelink).

options.text: Create an interface endpoint for DynamoDB in the VPC, and send the requests of the data center servers to it over Direct Connect.
options.why: For on-premises access [you must use AWS PrivateLink](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-faq-gateway-endpoint-limits-use-privatelink), which uses [interface VPC endpoints and private IP addresses](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-faq-privatelink-interface-endpoints).

options.text: Create an interface endpoint for DynamoDB in the VPC, and send the requests of both the applications and the data center servers to it.
options.why: This works, but PrivateLink is [available for an additional cost](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-faq-gateway-vs-privatelink-cost-note), and the daily terabytes of the applications can use a gateway endpoint without that cost.

items.explanation: The two groups of callers need two endpoint types. In the VPC, a gateway endpoint has [no additional charge for using gateway endpoints](../facts/vpc-endpoints.md#vpc-endpoints-wp-gateway-endpoint-no-additional-charge). Gateway endpoints do not serve the data center, so [you must use AWS PrivateLink](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-faq-gateway-endpoint-limits-use-privatelink), which reaches DynamoDB through [interface VPC endpoints and private IP addresses](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-faq-privatelink-interface-endpoints).
items.takeaway: VPC callers use the gateway endpoint at no extra charge; data center callers use an interface endpoint.
items.twin: If the stem said "only the applications in the VPC use the table" instead: the gateway endpoint alone, because there is [no additional charge for using gateway endpoints](../facts/vpc-endpoints.md#vpc-endpoints-wp-gateway-endpoint-no-additional-charge).
items.say: Inside the VPC I use the gateway endpoint at no extra charge; from the data center I use an interface endpoint.

steps: I read the last sentence first: it asks for two actions that keep all DynamoDB traffic private at the lowest cost.
I mark the constraints: applications in private subnets that move terabytes each day, servers in the data center behind Direct Connect, no public internet, and MOST cost-effectively.
Before I look at the options, I predict one interface endpoint for DynamoDB for everything, because PrivateLink serves both the VPC and the data center through private IP addresses.

I remove the NAT gateways, because a gateway endpoint reaches DynamoDB without a NAT device and NAT gateways charge for every gigabyte. I remove the data center route to the gateway endpoint, because gateway endpoints do not allow access from on-premises networks.

Between one interface endpoint for all callers and a gateway endpoint plus an interface endpoint, the difference is cost. My first idea breaks because the applications in the VPC can use a gateway endpoint at no additional charge, and PrivateLink is available for an additional cost.
Check: the gateway endpoint serves the applications at no extra charge, the interface endpoint serves the data center servers, and no request uses the public internet. Time: 90 seconds.

solvers.stem_only: Use a free gateway endpoint for DynamoDB in the route tables of the private subnets for the high-volume VPC traffic. Gateway endpoints cannot be reached from on premises, so add an interface endpoint (AWS PrivateLink) for DynamoDB and send only the low-volume data center traffic to it over Direct Connect.

items.stem: A company stores the order data of its online store in an Amazon DynamoDB table. The table uses provisioned capacity mode with auto scaling. Traffic is steady-state and predictable: the table uses almost all of its provisioned capacity around the clock. The company wants to keep requests from being throttled and wants to lower the monthly cost of the table. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?
keywords: almost all of its provisioned capacity

options.text: Change the table to on-demand capacity mode, so that DynamoDB bills each read and write request that the application makes.
options.why: At steady, high use, on-demand is not the cheaper mode: it costs less when the average utilization is [below 35%](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-ondemand-cheaper-below-35-percent-utilization).

options.text: Keep provisioned capacity mode with auto scaling, and purchase reserved capacity for the base level of reads and writes of the table.
options.why: Provisioned mode fits a [more steady and predictable usage pattern](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-provisioned-ideal-steady-predictable-usage), and reserved capacity, bought with a [one-time partial upfront payment](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-reserved-capacity-terms-and-discount), lowers the rate of that load.

options.text: Keep provisioned capacity mode with auto scaling, and add a DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster in front of the table for all requests.
options.why: With DAX, data is [first written to the DynamoDB table](../facts/dax.md#dax-write-through-both-table-and-dax), so the cluster adds cost and every write still uses the capacity of the table.

options.text: Keep provisioned capacity mode, turn off auto scaling, and set the read and write capacity to the highest level that the table has used.
options.why: Fixed capacity at the peak pays the standard rate for the [hourly read and write capacity you have provisioned](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-provisioned-billing-basis), with no reserved discount.
options.misconception: Turning off auto scaling at the peak level is the cheapest setup for a steady table.

items.explanation: The table uses almost all of its provisioned capacity all day. An ideal workload for provisioned mode has a [more steady and predictable usage pattern](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-provisioned-ideal-steady-predictable-usage), and on-demand costs less when average utilization is [below 35%](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-ondemand-cheaper-below-35-percent-utilization) or has quiet periods. This table runs near full use all day, so reserved capacity lowers the rate of the base load.
items.takeaway: Steady, predictable DynamoDB traffic near the provisioned level: provisioned mode plus reserved capacity.
items.twin: If the stem said "Traffic is unpredictable: the table sits idle for hours, then spikes to earlier peak levels within minutes." instead: on-demand capacity mode, because it is [billed per read or write request](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-ondemand-billed-per-request-zero-traffic-free).
items.say: Steady traffic that fills the provisioned capacity stays in provisioned mode, and reserved capacity lowers the rate.

solvers.stem_only: Steady, predictable, fully used provisioned capacity: keep provisioned mode and buy DynamoDB reserved capacity for the base level.

items.stem: A company runs its order service in us-east-1 and stores the orders in an Amazon DynamoDB table in on-demand capacity mode in the same Region. The company is planning cross-Region disaster recovery for a failure of the whole Region. If us-east-1 fails, a restore in us-west-2 within hours is acceptable, and so is losing up to 2 hours of data. Which solution meets these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?
keywords: a restore in us-west-2 within hours is acceptable
losing up to 2 hours of data

options.text: Convert the table into a global table, and add a replica table in us-west-2 that the application can read from and write to.
options.why: It works, but the replica table bills [one rWRU per replica table](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-gt-rwru-per-replica) for every write all day, for a recovery speed that the stem does not ask for.

options.text: Use AWS Backup to back up the table every hour, and copy each backup to a backup vault in us-west-2 for restores.
options.why: AWS Backup plans can copy backups across Regions [every hour, every 12 hours, daily, weekly, or monthly](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-dr-aws-backup-rpo-1-hour), and the hourly copy gives an [RPO of 1 hour](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-dr-aws-backup-rpo-1-hour), inside the 2 hours allowed.

options.text: Convert the table into a global table, and add replica tables in us-west-2 and in eu-west-1 that the application can read from and write to.
options.why: It works, but two replica tables each bill [one rWRU per replica table](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-gt-rwru-per-replica) for every write, far more than hourly backups cost.

options.text: Create a DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) cluster in us-west-2 that caches the items of the table and serves them to the application during an outage.
options.why: A DAX cluster can work only with [tables that are in the same Region](../facts/dax.md#dax-same-region-as-tables), so a cluster in us-west-2 cannot serve this table.
options.misconception: believes that a cache in another Region can stand in for the table

items.explanation: The stem accepts 2 hours of data loss and a restore that takes hours, so continuous replication is not needed. Hourly AWS Backup copies to us-west-2 give an [RPO of 1 hour](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-dr-aws-backup-rpo-1-hour), which leaves time for each copy to finish. After an outage, you restore the [entire table data to a new table](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-backup-restore-only-to-new-table) in us-west-2.
items.takeaway: When hours of recovery and hours of data loss are acceptable, cross-Region backups cost less than a global table.
items.twin: If the stem said "If us-east-1 fails, users must keep reading and writing orders in us-west-2 immediately, with no restore step." instead: a global table, because it gives an [RTO of zero](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-dr-global-tables-mrec-rto-zero).

solvers.stem_only: RPO of 2 hours and RTO of hours allow backup and restore, the cheapest DR strategy: schedule AWS Backup backups of the table at least hourly with a cross-Region copy to a vault in us-west-2, and restore there on failure. Global tables would work but cost far more.

items.stem: An online store keeps its orders in an Amazon DynamoDB table in provisioned capacity mode, and a mission-critical checkout API reads and writes items in the table. Two other workloads use most of the read capacity. A status page calls GetItem with strongly consistent reads for single orders, and the page can show data that is a few seconds old. Each night, a report job runs a Scan of the whole table with a filter expression that returns the orders whose status is OPEN; few orders are open at any time. The reads of the checkout API are throttled. Which TWO actions will reduce the read capacity that the two workloads consume with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)
keywords: can show data that is a few seconds old
returns the orders whose status is OPEN
few orders are open at any time

options.text: Make the filter expression of the nightly Scan more selective, so that the Scan returns fewer order items to the report job.
options.why: A filter runs after the read, so the Scan still [consumes the same amount of read capacity](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-scan-filter-same-read-capacity) as without it.

options.text: Add an attribute that only open orders carry, create a global secondary index on that attribute, and change the report job to query that index.
options.why: The index [only tracks data items](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-gsi-only-items-with-key-attributes) that carry its key, so it is [faster and less expensive to query that index](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-sparse-index-faster-cheaper-than-scan), and [DynamoDB maintains indexes automatically](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-indexes-maintained-automatically).

options.text: Create a DAX cluster, and send the strongly consistent GetItem calls of the status page through the DAX client so that DAX serves them from memory.
options.why: [DAX passes strongly consistent read requests to DynamoDB](../facts/dax.md#dax-passes-through-strong-reads-and-transactions) without a cache, so the table still serves every one of these reads.

options.text: Change the GetItem calls of the status page from strongly consistent reads to eventually consistent reads by setting ConsistentRead to false.
options.why: [Eventually consistent reads](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-eventually-consistent-half-cost) cost [half the cost of strongly consistent reads](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-eventually-consistent-half-cost), and the page accepts older data.

options.text: Copy each open order into a second table with a Lambda function on the stream of the table, and change the report job to scan the second table.
options.why: It also lowers the reads of the table, but the company must then run copy code and a second table, while [DynamoDB maintains indexes automatically](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-indexes-maintained-automatically).
options.misconception: A copy that custom code keeps in sync is the simplest way to take a report off a table.

items.explanation: Each workload needs its own fix. The report filters after it reads, so it [consumes the same amount of read capacity](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-scan-filter-same-read-capacity) as an unfiltered Scan; a sparse index [only tracks data items](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-gsi-only-items-with-key-attributes) that carry its key attribute. A synced copy table also works, but [DynamoDB maintains indexes automatically](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-indexes-maintained-automatically). The status page accepts older data, and [Eventually consistent reads](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-eventually-consistent-half-cost) cost half as much.
items.takeaway: Filters and DAX do not cut these reads; a sparse index and eventually consistent reads do.
items.twin: If the stem said "the status page must show the latest write" instead: keep its strongly consistent reads, because they return the [most up-to-date data](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-consistentread-parameter).
items.say: For the report I query a sparse index, and for the status page I use eventually consistent reads.

solvers.stem_only: Status page: switch its GetItem calls to eventually consistent reads, which cost half the read capacity of strongly consistent reads and fit data a few seconds old. Nightly report: a filter expression is applied after the read, so the Scan still consumes capacity for the whole table; use a sparse global secondary index on an attribute that only open orders carry and query the index (its reads use the index capacity, not the table's).

solvers.flag: Option D (copy open orders to a second table with a stream-triggered Lambda) also removes the scan reads from the main table, so only the unmeasured claim that a sparse GSI has less operational overhead separates E from D.

items.stem: A company runs a voting application on an Amazon DynamoDB table in provisioned capacity mode. The table holds one item for each contest, and the contest ID is the only key attribute. Each vote adds 1 to a counter attribute of that item with an UpdateItem call, and the item is smaller than 1 KB. The application reads the total of each contest every second to show it on screen. During a televised final, almost every vote is for one contest, at about 4,000 votes each second. Amazon CloudWatch shows that consumed write capacity is far below the provisioned write capacity, but many vote updates are throttled. Which solution will BEST resolve the throttling?
keywords: almost every vote is for one contest
far below the provisioned write capacity

options.text: Raise the provisioned write capacity of the table to several times the current peak, and keep one counter item for each contest in the table.
options.why: The table already has spare capacity; the limit is the partition of the hot item, which delivers at most [1,000 write units per second](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-partition-max-throughput).

options.text: Switch the table to on-demand capacity mode so that DynamoDB adds capacity during the burst, and keep one counter item for each contest in the table.
options.why: Every partition keeps its ceiling of [1,000 write units per second](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-partition-max-throughput) in either mode, and the hash of one key [determines the partition](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-partition-key-hash-decides-partition) of the hot item.
options.misconception: On-demand mode lifts the write ceiling of the partition that holds one hot item.

options.text: Write each vote as a new item with a unique vote ID as the key, and compute the total of each contest with a Scan that filters on the contest ID.
options.why: It stops the throttling, but a Scan [reads every item in a table](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-scan-reads-every-item), so each total on screen reads every vote of every contest.

options.text: Keep several counter items for each contest, with a random suffix from a fixed range added to the contest ID, and add up the counters for the total.
options.why: Random suffixes [randomize the writes across the larger space](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-write-sharding-random-suffix) of keys, so each vote updates one of several counter items.

items.explanation: Consumed capacity is far below provisioned capacity, so the table is not short of capacity; one item is. A hash of its key [determines the partition](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-partition-key-hash-decides-partition), and a partition delivers at most [1,000 write units per second](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-partition-max-throughput). Write sharding is to [add a random number](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-write-sharding-random-suffix) to the key, and the total then needs to [query the items for all the suffixes](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-write-sharding-read-merge) and add them up.
items.takeaway: Throttling on one item while the table has spare capacity means a hot key: shard it with a random suffix.
items.twin: If the stem said "consumed write capacity equals the provisioned write capacity, and the votes are spread across many contests" instead: raise the provisioned write capacity, because the whole table is short of capacity.
items.say: Spare table capacity plus throttling means one hot item, so I'd shard the counter with a random suffix.

steps: I read the last sentence first: it asks for the solution that BEST resolves the throttling of the vote updates.

I mark the constraints: one counter item for each contest, about 4,000 small updates each second on one item, consumed write capacity far below the provisioned capacity, and a total that the screen reads every second.
Before I look at the options, I predict write sharding, because throttling with spare table capacity points to one hot item, and the hash of one key decides one partition.

I remove the higher provisioned capacity, because the table already has spare capacity and each partition has its own ceiling. I remove on-demand mode, because the hot item stays in one partition with the same ceiling.

Between one item for each vote with a Scan and several counters with random suffixes, the difference is how the total is read; the stem says the screen reads the total every second, so a Scan of every vote each second is the weaker design.
Check: random suffixes spread the updates over several counter items, the total adds a few counters, and every constraint is met. Time: 90 seconds.

solvers.stem_only: This is a hot key: all writes go to one item, so one partition receives far more writes than its per-partition write limit, even though table-level capacity is unused. Raising table capacity or switching to on-demand does not lift the per-partition limit. Use write sharding: spread each contest's counter over several items with a calculated or random suffix on the key, and sum the shards when reading the total.

items.stem: A company stores the details of customer support calls in an Amazon DynamoDB table. Each item is a few KB, and the application reads the items often by call ID. The company now must also retain the audio recording of each call. Each recording is several MB, and agents open a recording only when a customer complains. The application must find the recording of a call from the item of that call. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?
keywords: find the recording of a call from the item

options.text: Store each recording as a binary attribute in the item of the call, and read the item with a projection expression when the application needs the details.
options.why: An item holds at most [400 KB](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-item-size-max), attribute names and values together, so a recording of several MB does not fit in one item.
options.misconception: A DynamoDB item can hold a file of any size.

options.text: Split each recording into parts that fit in an item, store the parts as items under the call ID, and read the parts back in order.
options.why: It can work, but a write unit covers an item [up to 1 KB](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-write-unit-1kb), so each recording costs many write units and many reads to rebuild.
options.misconception: Splitting a large file over many items is the cheapest way to keep it with its record.

options.text: Store each recording as an object in an Amazon S3 bucket, and save the S3 object key as an attribute in the item of that call.
options.why: AWS names the better pattern: [store pointers to Amazon S3 objects](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-faq-blob-use-s3-pointers) in the table, so each item stays small and cheap to read.

options.text: Store each recording in an Amazon ElastiCache cluster with the call ID as the key, and keep the call details in the DynamoDB table.
options.why: ElastiCache is an [ephemeral cache for frequently accessed data](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-decision-guide-elasticache-caching-layer), not a store that retains rarely opened recordings.

items.explanation: A recording is far larger than one item, which holds at most [400 KB](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-item-size-max). AWS says a better pattern is to [store pointers to Amazon S3 objects](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-faq-blob-use-s3-pointers) in the table: you [store the Amazon S3 object identifier](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-large-items-store-in-s3) in the item. The application reads the small item often and fetches a recording from S3 when an agent opens it.
items.takeaway: A file larger than an item goes to Amazon S3, and the item keeps the object key.
items.twin: If the stem said "each recording is a short text summary of a few KB" instead: keep it as an attribute of the item, because it fits within [400 KB](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-item-size-max).
items.say: Big files go to S3, and the DynamoDB item keeps a pointer to the object.

steps: I read the last sentence first: it asks for the MOST cost-effective way to keep a large recording with each call record.
I mark the constraints: items of a few KB that the application reads often, recordings of several MB that agents open rarely, every recording retained, and a way from each item to its recording.
Before I look at the options, I predict Amazon S3 for the recordings with a pointer in each item, because an item holds at most 400 KB.
I remove the binary attribute, because a recording of several MB does not fit in one item. I remove ElastiCache, because it is an ephemeral cache, not a store that retains data.

Between splitting each recording into many items and storing it in S3 with a pointer, the difference is cost; the stem says MOST cost-effective, so many write units for each recording lose to one small attribute.
Check: S3 keeps each recording, the item stores the object key, reads of the details stay small, and every constraint is met. Time: 90 seconds.

solvers.stem_only: Recordings of several MB exceed the DynamoDB item size limit and are rarely read; store them as objects in Amazon S3 (with a low-cost storage class or lifecycle if desired) and keep the S3 object key in the DynamoDB item as a pointer.

items.stem: A company keeps customer profiles in an Amazon DynamoDB table in provisioned capacity mode, and several support agents can edit the same profile. The application reads the profile item, changes attributes such as the address and the phone number, and writes the whole item back with PutItem. Sometimes two agents save the same profile at almost the same time, and the change of the first agent is lost without an error. The application must detect such a conflict so that the second agent reloads the profile. Agents save thousands of profiles each hour, and the company wants each save to consume as little write capacity as possible. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?
keywords: writes the whole item back with PutItem
as little write capacity as possible

options.text: Add a version attribute to each profile item, increase it on each save, and make each PutItem call conditional on the version that was read.
options.why: Each item gets a [version attribute that increments with every update](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-optimistic-locking-detects-conflicts-at-write), and the write fails when [another process modified the item in the meantime](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-optimistic-locking-condition-fails-on-concurrent-change).

options.text: Send each save as a TransactWriteItems call that holds one Put action with a condition on a version attribute of the profile item.
options.why: It detects the conflict too, but each item in a write transaction requires [two write capacity units](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-transaction-two-units-prepare-commit), twice the cost of one conditional write.
options.misconception: A transaction is needed to protect a write to a single item.

options.text: Send each save of a profile through a BatchWriteItem call instead of PutItem, so that DynamoDB applies all the changes of the save as one unit.
options.why: A batch is not a transaction, and [only some of the actions](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-transactwriteitems-vs-batchwriteitem) might succeed; nothing compares versions, so the second save still replaces the first.

options.text: Read the profile item with a strongly consistent read right before each PutItem call, and keep writing the whole item back without a condition.
options.why: Another save can land between the read and the write, and PutItem is [unconditional](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-writes-unconditional-by-default): it [overwrites an existing item](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-writes-unconditional-by-default) with the same key.
options.misconception: A fresh read right before a write prevents a lost update.

items.explanation: PutItem is [unconditional](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-writes-unconditional-by-default), so the second save [overwrites an existing item](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-writes-unconditional-by-default). Optimistic locking [detects conflicts at write time](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-optimistic-locking-detects-conflicts-at-write): the condition fails when [another process modified the item in the meantime](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-optimistic-locking-condition-fails-on-concurrent-change), and the second agent reloads. A transaction also detects it, but each item in it requires [two write capacity units](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-transaction-two-units-prepare-commit), so one conditional write uses less write capacity.
items.takeaway: To catch a lost update on one item, make the write conditional on a version attribute.
items.twin: If the stem said "the debit of one item and the credit of another item must both happen or neither" instead: use TransactWriteItems, because it gives a [guaranteed all-or-nothing result](../facts/dynamodb.md#dynamodb-transactwriteitems-all-or-nothing).
items.say: I'd add a version attribute and make the write conditional, so a stale save fails instead of overwriting.

solvers.stem_only: Optimistic locking: add a version number attribute, increment it on each save, and make PutItem conditional (condition expression) on the version that was read; a failed condition (ConditionalCheckFailedException) tells the second agent to reload. A plain conditional write costs normal write units, whereas a transaction costs twice as much and BatchWriteItem has no conditions.
